items.prompt: Why can gradient-based fitting of (unregularized) logistic regression not get stuck in a spurious local minimum?
choices: The negative log-likelihood is a convex function of the weights
The sigmoid makes the model a linear function of the weights
The loss has a closed-form minimizer, as least squares does
Gradient descent finds a global minimum of any smooth loss function
items.explain: The logistic negative log-likelihood is convex in w (its Hessian XᵀSX, with S = diag(pᵢ(1 − pᵢ)), is positive semidefinite), so every local minimum is global. There is no closed form; it is solved iteratively, e.g. by Newton/IRLS.

items.prompt: In the dual of a soft-margin SVM, which training points can receive nonzero dual coefficients αᵢ?
choices: Every training point, with equal weight
Points on the margin, inside it, or misclassified
Only the misclassified training points
The points farthest from the decision boundary on each side
items.explain: By complementary slackness, αᵢ > 0 only where the margin constraint is active or violated; these are the support vectors (a point exactly on the margin may still have αᵢ = 0). Points safely outside the margin have αᵢ = 0 and do not affect the solution.

items.prompt: For an inequality constraint g(x) ≤ 0 with Lagrange multiplier μ, what do the KKT conditions require of μ at an optimum?
choices: μ ≥ 0 and μ·g(x) = 0
μ = 0 whenever g(x) = 0
μ ≤ 0 and μ·g(x) ≥ 0
μ > 0 for every constraint
items.explain: Dual feasibility requires μ ≥ 0 and complementary slackness requires μ·g(x) = 0: a constraint that is slack (g < 0) has zero multiplier, and only active constraints can have μ > 0.

items.prompt: Linear MPC with a quadratic cost, linear dynamics and linear (polyhedral) state and input constraints solves which kind of problem at each step?
choices: A mixed-integer linear program
A nonconvex nonlinear program
An unconstrained least-squares fit
A convex quadratic program
items.explain: Stacking the predicted states as linear functions of the input sequence turns the cost into a convex quadratic and the constraints into linear inequalities: a QP, solvable reliably in real time.

items.prompt: Gradient descent minimizes a quadratic whose Hessian has eigenvalues between μ > 0 and L. What most directly makes convergence slow?
choices: A large smallest eigenvalue μ
A large number of data points
A Hessian that is positive definite
A large condition number κ = L/μ
items.explain: With the best fixed step, the error contracts per step by about (κ − 1)/(κ + 1), so ill-conditioning (κ ≫ 1) makes progress along the flat directions very slow. Ridge's λ raises μ and so improves κ.

items.prompt: Under gradient flow dθ/dt = −∇L(θ), how does the loss change along a trajectory?
choices: dL/dt = −‖∇L(θ)‖², so it never increases
dL/dt = −L(θ), so it decays exponentially
dL/dt = −‖θ‖², so it shrinks with the weights
It may rise or fall, depending on curvature
items.explain: By the chain rule dL/dt = ∇L·dθ/dt = −‖∇L‖² ≤ 0. Gradient flow is monotone; non-monotone loss curves come from finite step sizes or noise, not from the flow itself.

items.prompt: Gradient descent with step size η on f(w) = ½·a·w² with a = 4. For which η does wₖ converge to 0?
items.explain: The update is wₖ₊₁ = (1 − 4η)wₖ, which converges iff |1 − 4η| < 1, i.e. 0 < η < 2/a = 0.5. The value 0.25 = 1/a is the fastest (one-step) choice, not the stability limit.

items.prompt: Proximal gradient methods for the lasso apply the proximal operator of λ|w| coordinatewise. What does it map a value v to?
choices: sign(v)·max(|v| − λ, 0)
v when |v| > λ, and 0 otherwise
max(v − λ, 0)
items.explain: The L1 prox is soft-thresholding: it shrinks v toward zero by λ and sets it exactly to zero when |v| ≤ λ, which is what produces sparsity. v/(1 + λ) is the prox of the ridge penalty (λ/2)w², and the keep-or-kill rule is hard thresholding.

items.prompt: Why is the SVM dual problem the natural place to apply the kernel trick?
choices: The dual has fewer variables than features in every problem
The dual objective is linear, so any kernel keeps it easy to solve
The dual removes the box constraints 0 ≤ αᵢ ≤ C on the multipliers
Data enter only via inner products xᵢᵀxⱼ, replaceable by k(xᵢ, xⱼ)
items.explain: In the dual, both the objective and the decision function depend on the data only through inner products, so swapping in a positive-definite kernel fits a linear separator in feature space without forming features. The dual is a QP with one variable per training point and keeps its box constraints.

items.prompt: How is discrete-time, finite-horizon LQR solved exactly?
choices: A backward Riccati recursion (dynamic programming) with time-varying gains
Gradient descent on one constant gain matrix, iterated forward in time from the initial state
A single linear program over the entire input sequence and horizon
Pole placement repeated independently at every step of the horizon
items.explain: The value function stays quadratic, Vₖ(x) = xᵀPₖx, so Bellman's recursion reduces to a backward Riccati difference equation for Pₖ; the optimal input is uₖ = −Kₖxₖ with gains that vary over the horizon.

items.prompt: With pᵢ = σ(wᵀxᵢ) and labels yᵢ ∈ {0, 1}, what is the gradient of the logistic negative log-likelihood?
choices: Σᵢ (yᵢ − pᵢ) pᵢ xᵢ
Σᵢ pᵢ(1 − pᵢ) xᵢ
Σᵢ (pᵢ − yᵢ) xᵢ
Σᵢ (pᵢ − yᵢ)² xᵢ
items.explain: The sigmoid's derivative cancels against the log, leaving residual times input, ∇ = Σ(pᵢ − yᵢ)xᵢ, the same form as least squares. The term pᵢ(1 − pᵢ) appears in the Hessian, not the gradient.

items.prompt: LMS is stochastic gradient descent on mean-squared error with input autocorrelation matrix R. For convergence of the mean weights, the step size μ must satisfy what?
choices: 0 < μ < 2/λmax(R)
0 < μ < 2/λmin(R)
0 < μ < 1/trace(R)²
0 < μ < λmax(R)/2
items.explain: The mean weight error evolves as (I − μR)ᵏ, which shrinks iff |1 − μλᵢ| < 1 for every eigenvalue, i.e. μ < 2/λmax. The bound is set by the largest eigenvalue; the smallest one sets how slowly the slowest mode converges.

items.prompt: The squared loss of a deep linear network W_L⋯W₁ is nonconvex in its weights. Which statement is true of its critical points (Kawaguchi, 2016)?
choices: The loss is convex, since the end-to-end map is linear
Spurious local minima exist, one per subset of singular modes
The only critical points are global minima, so no saddles exist
Every local minimum is global; other critical points are saddles
items.explain: Kawaguchi proved that for deep linear networks every local minimum is a global minimum and every other critical point is a saddle (some, for depth > 3, without negative curvature). For example W = 0 is a saddle, which is why small initialization produces plateaus.

items.prompt: In the NTK regime, gradient flow on squared loss evolves the training residual as dr/dt = −ηΘr with a fixed Gram matrix Θ. Which part of the residual is fit slowest?
choices: The component along Θ's largest-eigenvalue eigenvectors
The component along Θ's smallest-eigenvalue eigenvectors
All components equally, at a rate set by η alone
The component along the target vector y itself
items.explain: In Θ's eigenbasis each component decays as exp(−ηλᵢt), so small-eigenvalue directions are learned slowest. Jacot et al. note that convergence is fastest along the top kernel principal components, which motivates early stopping.

items.prompt: For linear MPC with a strictly convex quadratic cost and polyhedral constraints, what form does the optimal first input u*(x) take as a function of the current state over the feasible set (explicit MPC)?
choices: Linear everywhere, equal to the unconstrained LQR gain
Continuous and piecewise affine over a polyhedral partition
Piecewise constant and discontinuous across regions
A smooth, infinitely differentiable nonlinear map
items.explain: The QP is a multiparametric program in x. Bemporad et al. (2002) show that when its Hessian in the inputs is positive definite, u*(x) is continuous and piecewise affine over a polyhedral partition of the feasible states: affine within each region of fixed active constraints, and in the region with none active a single linear gain (the LQR gain when the terminal cost is the Riccati solution).

items.prompt: Unregularized logistic regression is trained by gradient descent on linearly separable data. What happens to the weights w?
choices: w converges to a finite maximum-likelihood estimate that separates the data
‖w‖ → ∞ while w/‖w‖ tends to the max-margin (hard-SVM) direction
w converges to the least-squares solution on the 0/1 labels
‖w‖ stays bounded while its direction keeps oscillating among separators
items.explain: On separable data the loss can be driven toward zero only by scaling w up, so no finite minimizer exists. Soudry et al. show that the direction converges, slowly (logarithmically), to the L2 max-margin separator: an implicit bias of gradient descent.

items.prompt: The LQR cost J(K) of a static gain u = −Kx, averaged over random initial states with full-rank covariance, is nonconvex in K, yet policy gradient converges globally to the optimal gain (Fazel et al., 2018). What makes this possible?
choices: J(K) is in fact convex over the set of stabilizing gains
The set of stabilizing gains is convex, so projected gradient steps suffice
Every local minimum of J stabilizes, so any of them is acceptable
J obeys gradient domination: J(K) − J* ≤ c‖∇J(K)‖² on stabilizing K
items.explain: Fazel et al. prove a Polyak–Łojasiewicz-type gradient-domination bound J(K) − J* ≤ c‖∇J(K)‖_F² over stabilizing gains, with c set by the optimal gain's state covariance, σmin(E[x₀x₀ᵀ]) > 0 and σmin(R). So every stationary stabilizing gain is optimal, and small gradient steps from a stabilizing start converge linearly. Neither J nor the stabilizing set is convex in general.

items.prompt: Cohen et al. (2021) trained neural networks with full-batch gradient descent at step size η. What did the sharpness (top Hessian eigenvalue) typically do?
choices: It stayed safely below 2/η throughout, as classical step-size analysis requires
It rose past 2/η and training diverged soon afterward
It rose to about 2/η and hovered there while loss still fell over time
It fell steadily toward zero as training progressed
items.explain: They call this the Edge of Stability: sharpness increases (progressive sharpening) until it reaches about 2/η, then hovers just above it; the loss is non-monotone over short spans but keeps decreasing over long ones, contrary to the quadratic picture in which λ > 2/η means divergence.

items.prompt: A density pₜ(x) is transported by a velocity field vₜ(x) with no mass created or destroyed. Which equation does it satisfy?
choices: ∂p/∂t + ∇·(p v) = Δp
items.explain: Conservation of mass gives the continuity equation ∂p/∂t + ∇·(pv) = 0. It expands to v·∇p + p∇·v, so dropping either term is only right for divergence-free or spatially uniform cases. A Δp term would add diffusion, which pure transport does not have.

items.prompt: What is one explicit Euler step of size Δt for dh/dt = f(h, t)?
choices: h(t + Δt) ≈ h(t) + Δt·f(h(t), t)
h(t + Δt) ≈ h(t) + f(h(t), t)/Δt
h(t + Δt) ≈ h(t) + Δt·f(h(t + Δt), t + Δt)
h(t + Δt) ≈ Δt·h(t) + f(h(t), t)
items.explain: Explicit Euler follows the current slope for one step. Evaluating f at the new point is implicit (backward) Euler, which needs a solve; a residual block h + f(h) is an Euler step with Δt = 1.

items.prompt: Besides the energy H, which quantity does every exact Hamiltonian flow preserve?
choices: The kinetic energy and the potential energy separately
The distance between any two trajectories
Phase-space volume (Liouville's theorem)
Each momentum coordinate pᵢ individually
items.explain: Hamiltonian vector fields are divergence-free in (q, p), so they preserve phase-space volume (indeed the symplectic form). Kinetic and potential energy trade off, nearby trajectories can separate, and momenta change under forces.

items.prompt: At an equilibrium x* of ẋ = f(x), which condition on the Jacobian Df(x*) guarantees local asymptotic stability?
choices: All eigenvalues have magnitude less than 1
All eigenvalues are real numbers
The determinant of Df(x*) is negative
All eigenvalues have negative real parts
items.explain: If Df(x*) is Hurwitz, the linearization decays and so does the nonlinear system near x*. Magnitude below 1 is the discrete-time (map) condition; complex eigenvalues with negative real part give stable spirals.

items.prompt: A PINN u_θ(x, t) is trained on the heat equation u_t = u_xx. What is the residual penalized at a collocation point?
choices: ∂u_θ/∂t − ∂²u_θ/∂x², obtained by automatic differentiation
u_θ(x, t) minus a measured temperature at that collocation point
∂u_θ/∂t + ∂²u_θ/∂x², from finite differences on a grid
∂²u_θ/∂t² − ∂u_θ/∂x, from automatic differentiation
items.explain: The PDE residual is the equation moved to one side, u_t − u_xx, evaluated by differentiating the network itself; no labels or grid are needed at collocation points. Data misfit terms are separate (initial, boundary or observation losses).

items.prompt: Under the Fourier transform (convention e^(−iωt)), what does time differentiation d/dt become?
choices: Multiplication by 1/(iω)
Convolution with iω
Multiplication by iω
Multiplication by −ω²
items.explain: Differentiating e^(iωt) multiplies it by iω, so d/dt becomes multiplication by iω and linear constant-coefficient ODEs become algebraic. −ω² is the factor for the second derivative and 1/(iω) corresponds to integration.

items.prompt: For a continuous normalizing flow dh/dt = f(h, t), how does the log-density of a sample evolve along its trajectory?
choices: d log p(h(t))/dt = −tr(∂f/∂h)
d log p(h(t))/dt = +tr(∂f/∂h)
d log p(h(t))/dt = −log|det(∂f/∂h)|
d log p(h(t))/dt = −‖f(h, t)‖²
items.explain: The instantaneous change-of-variables formula replaces the log-determinant of a discrete flow with the trace of the Jacobian. Expanding flow (positive divergence) spreads mass, so log-density decreases.

items.prompt: Explicit Euler with step h is applied to the stiff test equation ẋ = −λx with λ = 1000. For which h does the numerical solution decay to zero?
choices: Any h > 0
items.explain: Each step multiplies x by (1 − hλ), which decays iff |1 − hλ| < 1, i.e. 0 < h < 2/λ = 0.002. Fast decaying modes force tiny steps on explicit solvers (adaptive ones just shrink h to stay stable), which is why stiff systems call for implicit, A-stable solvers.

items.prompt: The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck SDE dx = −θx dt + σ dW (θ > 0) underlies the variance-preserving diffusion. What is its stationary variance?
choices: σ²/(2θ)
σ²/(2θ²)
σ²
items.explain: Variance obeys dv/dt = −2θv + σ², whose fixed point is σ²/(2θ). With θ = 1 and σ = √2 this gives unit variance, which is why such forward processes end at N(0, I).

items.prompt: What do the trajectories of ẋ = Ax with A = [[0, 1], [−1, 0]] look like?
choices: Spirals that decay into the origin over time
Spirals that grow outward without bound
Circles around the origin (eigenvalues ±i)
Straight lines in and out of a saddle point
items.explain: The eigenvalues are ±i, purely imaginary, so solutions are rotations x(t) = (r cos(t + φ), −r sin(t + φ)) and d(x₁² + x₂²)/dt = 0. A center like this is the borderline case where linearization alone cannot settle stability for nonlinear systems.

items.prompt: In the adjoint method for neural ODEs, the adjoint a(t) = ∂L/∂h(t) is integrated backward in time. Which ODE does it satisfy?
choices: da/dt = +a(t)ᵀ ∂f/∂h
da/dt = −a(t)ᵀ ∂f/∂h
da/dt = −a(t)ᵀ ∂f/∂θ
da/dt = −f(h(t), t)
items.explain: Differentiating through the flow gives da/dt = −aᵀ∂f/∂h, solved from a(T) = ∂L/∂h(T) backward. The term aᵀ∂f/∂θ is the integrand that accumulates the parameter gradient, not the adjoint's own dynamics.

items.prompt: For the forward SDE dx = f(x, t) dt + g(t) dW, what is the drift of the probability-flow ODE that shares its marginals pₜ?
choices: dx/dt = f(x, t) − g(t)² ∇ₓ log pₜ(x)
dx/dt = f(x, t) + ½ g(t)² ∇ₓ log pₜ(x)
dx/dt = f(x, t) − ½ g(t) ∇ₓ log pₜ(x)
dx/dt = f(x, t) − ½ g(t)² ∇ₓ log pₜ(x)
items.explain: Writing the Fokker–Planck diffusion term as a transport term yields the drift f − ½g²∇log p. The full g² version is the drift of the reverse-time SDE, which also adds noise; both rely only on the score.

items.prompt: Over very long simulations, a symplectic integrator such as leapfrog keeps energy error bounded instead of drifting. Why?
choices: It conserves the true H exactly at every single step
Its steps track the exact flow of a modified Hamiltonian
It adapts its step size to cancel energy drift
Its local error is of higher order than RK4's
items.explain: Backward error analysis shows a symplectic map is, up to exponentially small error, the exact flow of a modified Hamiltonian H̃ = H + O(hᵖ), so H stays within O(hᵖ) of its start for exponentially long times. Leapfrog is only second order, and generic Runge–Kutta methods have no such conserved quantity.

items.prompt: Why can no neural ODE dh/dt = f(h) with Lipschitz f (no augmented dimensions) map every 1-D input x to −x at t = 1?
choices: Trajectories can't cross, so the flow preserves order on the line
The ODE solver's discretization error grows too large to flip a sign
Lipschitz vector fields can only produce contractions of the line
The adjoint method cannot compute gradients for this target map
items.explain: Uniqueness of solutions means two trajectories in ℝ¹ can never pass each other, so the time-1 flow is an increasing homeomorphism, while x ↦ −x reverses order. Dupont et al. show neural ODEs preserve input topology and lift the limit by augmenting the state.

items.prompt: For ẋ = −x³, linearization at 0 gives eigenvalue 0. What does V(x) = x² show?
choices: V̇ = −2x² < 0 for x ≠ 0, so 0 is exponentially stable
V̇ = 0 everywhere, so 0 is stable but not attractive
V̇ = −3x² < 0, so stability follows from the linearization
V̇ = −2x⁴ < 0 for x ≠ 0, so 0 is asymptotically stable
items.explain: V̇ = 2x·ẋ = −2x⁴, negative definite, so the origin is asymptotically stable. It is not exponentially stable: solutions decay like 1/√(2t), which is why the zero eigenvalue made linearization inconclusive.

items.prompt: A centered data matrix X (rows = samples) has SVD X = UΣVᵀ. Where are the principal directions?
choices: The columns of U
The columns of V
The diagonal entries of Σ
The rows of U
items.explain: XᵀX = VΣ²Vᵀ, so V's columns are eigenvectors of the (scaled) covariance, i.e. the principal directions. UΣ gives the sample scores, and σᵢ²/(n − 1) gives the variances.

items.prompt: In self-attention, Q and K are both n×d (n tokens, head dimension d). What is the shape of QKᵀ?
choices: d × d
n × d
n × n
d × n
items.explain: An (n×d)(d×n) product is n×n: one score for every pair of tokens. That n×n matrix is the source of attention's quadratic cost in sequence length.

items.prompt: Which property does every valid covariance matrix P (such as the Kalman filter's) have?
choices: Symmetric with all entries nonnegative
Symmetric positive semidefinite
Orthogonal, so that PᵀP = I
Diagonal in the state coordinates
items.explain: P = E[(x − m)(x − m)ᵀ] is symmetric, and vᵀPv = Var(vᵀx) ≥ 0. Off-diagonal entries can be negative (negative correlation), and correlated states make P non-diagonal.

items.prompt: In a Hankel matrix H, what does the entry H(i, j) depend on?
choices: Only the sum i + j
Only the difference i − j
Only the product i·j
Only the larger of i and j
items.explain: Hankel matrices are constant along anti-diagonals, H(i, j) = h(i + j), e.g. stacked Markov parameters CAⁱ⁺ʲB. Constant diagonals, depending on i − j, define a Toeplitz matrix instead.

items.prompt: A linear network computes W₂W₁x with W₁ of size h×n and W₂ of size m×h, where h < min(m, n). What is the largest possible rank of W₂W₁?
choices: min(m, n)
m + n − h
h
m·n/h
items.explain: rank(AB) ≤ min(rank A, rank B) ≤ h, so the hidden width is a bottleneck: the network can represent only rank-h linear maps, and from small initialization gradient descent learns the leading singular modes first.

items.prompt: Let J = m nᵀ/N with nonzero m, n ∈ ℝᴺ. What are its rank and its only possibly nonzero eigenvalue?
choices: Rank 1; eigenvalue nᵀm/N, with eigenvector m
Rank 1; eigenvalue ‖m‖‖n‖/N, with eigenvector n
Rank N; eigenvalues are mᵢnᵢ/N
Rank 2; eigenvalues ±‖m‖‖n‖/N
items.explain: Every column of J is a multiple of m, so rank is 1, and J m = m (nᵀm)/N. The overlap nᵀm, not the product of norms, sets the eigenvalue, which governs the stability of the collective mode in low-rank RNNs.

items.prompt: Which algebraic fact lets (non-causal) linear attention φ(Q)φ(K)ᵀV avoid forming an n×n matrix?
choices: Commutativity: φ(Q)φ(K)ᵀ equals φ(K)ᵀφ(Q), a d×d matrix
Orthogonality: φ(K) has orthonormal columns, so φ(K)ᵀφ(K) is the identity
Associativity: compute φ(K)ᵀV (d×d_v) first, then multiply by φ(Q)
Symmetry: φ(Q)φ(K)ᵀ is symmetric, so only half must be stored
items.explain: (φ(Q)φ(K)ᵀ)V = φ(Q)(φ(K)ᵀV), and the right grouping costs O(n·d·d_v), linear in n. Softmax applies a row-wise nonlinearity to QKᵀ, which blocks this regrouping.

items.prompt: A minimal n-state discrete LTI system has Markov parameters hₖ = CAᵏ⁻¹B. What is the rank of a large enough Hankel matrix built from them?
choices: The number of rows of the Hankel matrix
n
n²
items.explain: The Hankel matrix factors as (observability matrix)·(reachability matrix), both of rank n for a minimal system, so its rank is n. ERA reads the model order from this rank and builds A, B, C from the factors.

items.prompt: Dynamic mode decomposition fits x_{k+1} ≈ A xₖ from snapshot matrices X = [x₁ … x_{m−1}] and X′ = [x₂ … x_m]. Which A does it compute?
choices: A = X′X⁺, where X⁺ is the pseudoinverse of X
A = X⁺X′, where X⁺ is the pseudoinverse of X
A = XᵀX′, the cross-covariance of the snapshots
A = X X′⁺, where X′⁺ is the pseudoinverse of X′
items.explain: DMD solves the least-squares problem min ‖X′ − AX‖_F, whose minimum-norm solution is X′X⁺ (computed in practice through a truncated SVD of X). Its eigenvalues and eigenvectors approximate Koopman eigenvalues and modes.

items.prompt: A circular convolution of length N is multiplication by a circulant matrix C. What diagonalizes C?
choices: The identity, since C is already diagonal
A Householder reflection built from C's first column
The discrete Fourier transform matrix
Its own Cholesky factor
items.explain: Every circulant matrix has the Fourier vectors as eigenvectors, C = F⁻¹ diag(F c) F, with eigenvalues equal to the DFT of its first column c. This is the matrix form of the convolution theorem.

items.prompt: X has singular values σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ …. What is the best rank-k approximation in Frobenius norm, and its squared error?
choices: Truncated SVD; squared error σₖ₊₁²
The top-k rows of X; error Σᵢ₌ₖ₊₁ σᵢ
Truncated SVD; squared error Σᵢ₌ₖ₊₁ σᵢ²
Any rank-k projection; error σ₁ − σₖ
items.explain: By Eckart–Young, keeping the top k singular triplets is optimal and leaves the remaining energy Σᵢ>ₖ σᵢ² in the Frobenius norm. σₖ₊₁² is the squared error in the spectral (operator) norm, a different measure.

items.prompt: Why do robust Kalman implementations use the Joseph form P⁺ = (I − KH)P⁻(I − KH)ᵀ + KRKᵀ instead of P⁺ = (I − KH)P⁻?
choices: It needs fewer multiplications than the short form
It gives a more accurate posterior mean than the short form
It is required whenever the measurement matrix H is square
It stays symmetric PSD under rounding and for any gain K
items.explain: Both forms agree for the optimal gain in exact arithmetic, but the short form subtracts and can lose symmetry or positive semidefiniteness numerically. The Joseph form is a sum of PSD terms and is valid for any K, at extra cost.

items.prompt: By the PBH test, when is the LTI pair (A, B) uncontrollable?
choices: When A has an eigenvalue equal to zero
When B has fewer columns than A has rows
When at least one column of B is the zero vector
When some left eigenvector w of A has wᵀB = 0
items.explain: rank [A − λI, B] < n for some eigenvalue λ means a mode w with wᵀA = λwᵀ that the input never excites (wᵀB = 0). A single input can control many states, and a singular A is irrelevant.

items.prompt: Under a state change x̃ = Tx, the Gramians transform as Wc → T Wc Tᵀ and Wo → T⁻ᵀ Wo T⁻¹. Which quantity is invariant?
choices: The eigenvalues of Wc alone
The trace of Wo alone
The eigenvalues of Wc·Wo
The matrix Wc itself
items.explain: Wc·Wo maps to T(Wc Wo)T⁻¹, a similarity transform, so its eigenvalues (squared Hankel singular values) are coordinate-free. Each Gramian alone can be rescaled arbitrarily, which is why balancing makes them equal and diagonal before truncating.

items.prompt: What is the widely used simplified DDPM training loss?
choices: An adversarial loss against a discriminator on real versus generated images
Exact log-likelihood computed through an invertible change of variables
Encoder–decoder reconstruction error plus a KL penalty to a Gaussian prior
Mean squared error between the added noise ε and the predicted ε_θ(xₜ, t)
items.explain: Ho et al. found that a reweighted variational bound, ‖ε − ε_θ(√ᾱₜx₀ + √(1 − ᾱₜ)ε, t)‖², trains best; it is equivalent to denoising score matching. The other options describe GANs, normalizing flows and VAEs.

items.prompt: Why is sampling from a standard diffusion model slower than sampling from a GAN of similar size?
choices: Its network has far more parameters to evaluate
It must train a discriminator at sampling time
It needs many sequential network evaluations
It must invert a large Jacobian at every step
items.explain: Generation integrates a reverse process over tens to hundreds of denoising steps, each a full network pass, while a GAN generator maps noise to a sample in one pass. Faster samplers (DDIM, distillation, straighter flows) attack exactly this step count.

items.prompt: Peebles and Xie scaled diffusion transformers (DiTs). What relationship did they report between model compute and sample quality?
choices: FID improved with parameters but not with more input tokens
Larger DiTs overfit, so FID worsened beyond a moderate model size
FID depended on the patch size alone, not on depth or width
More forward-pass Gflops gave consistently lower (better) FID
items.explain: The DiT paper found FID falls consistently as forward-pass Gflops grow, whether from depth, width or more tokens (smaller patches); parameter count alone did not predict quality. DiT-XL/2 reached FID 2.27 on class-conditional ImageNet 256×256 with classifier-free guidance.

items.prompt: Denoising score matching perturbs data as x̃ = x + σε with ε ~ N(0, I). What target does the network s_θ(x̃) regress onto?
choices: ε/σ
−ε/σ
−σε
−ε/σ²
items.explain: The perturbation kernel's score is ∇ log N(x̃; x, σ²I) = −(x̃ − x)/σ² = −ε/σ, and regressing onto it recovers the score of the noised marginal. The sign matters: the score points back toward the clean data.

items.prompt: How do DDIM samplers relate to DDPM?
choices: A new training objective that has to be learned from scratch
Same training objective; non-Markovian forward processes permit far fewer steps
Same sampler, but with a learned variance schedule replacing a fixed one
A GAN-style discriminator added to sharpen samples in fewer denoising steps
items.explain: Song, Meng and Ermon build non-Markovian forward processes with the same marginals, hence the same training loss, so a pretrained DDPM can be sampled 10–50× faster with a short subsequence of steps; with η = 0 (σₜ = 0, no added noise) the sampler is deterministic.

items.prompt: Why does making the learned ODE paths straighter (as in rectified flow) speed up sampling?
choices: Straight paths make the training loss convex in the neural network weights
A straight path can be followed accurately with very few Euler steps
Straight paths remove the need for a source noise distribution
Straight paths let the sampler skip evaluating the vector field
items.explain: Discretization error comes from curvature: on an exactly straight path a single Euler step lands on the endpoint. Liu et al. use repeated rectification to straighten paths, reaching good samples with one or a few steps.

items.prompt: Entropy-regularized optimal transport between discrete marginals a and b, with cost C and regularization ε, has a solution of what form?
choices: A permutation matrix that pairs each source point with one target
π = diag(u)·K·diag(v) with K = exp(−C/ε), u and v scaled to fit a and b
π = a bᵀ, the independent coupling, for every ε > 0
π = exp(−C/ε) normalized to sum to 1, with no marginal constraints fitted
items.explain: The entropic term makes the optimal plan a diagonal scaling of the Gibbs kernel, and Sinkhorn alternately rescales u and v to match the marginals, far cheaper than a transport LP. As ε → 0 it approaches unregularized OT; as ε → ∞, a bᵀ.

items.prompt: For a variance-preserving diffusion xₜ = √ᾱₜ x₀ + √(1 − ᾱₜ) ε, how is the score of pₜ obtained from a trained noise predictor ε_θ?
choices: ∇ log pₜ(xₜ) ≈ −ε_θ(xₜ, t)·√(1 − ᾱₜ)
∇ log pₜ(xₜ) ≈ −ε_θ(xₜ, t)/√(1 − ᾱₜ)
∇ log pₜ(xₜ) ≈ −ε_θ(xₜ, t)/√ᾱₜ
∇ log pₜ(xₜ) ≈ +ε_θ(xₜ, t)/(1 − ᾱₜ)
items.explain: The conditional score is −(xₜ − √ᾱₜx₀)/(1 − ᾱₜ) = −ε/√(1 − ᾱₜ), and the noise predictor's optimum is E[ε | xₜ], so the score is −ε_θ/√(1 − ᾱₜ). This is the bridge between DDPM and score-SDE sampling.

items.prompt: Flow matching regresses onto conditional velocities uₜ(x | x₁) even though the target is the intractable marginal field uₜ(x). Why is that valid?
choices: Both losses have the same gradient in θ; they differ by a constant
The conditional velocity equals the marginal velocity at every x
Each data point x₁ gets its own model, later averaged together
Conditional paths are deterministic, so the loss has zero variance
items.explain: Lipman et al. show the conditional flow matching loss equals the marginal one up to a θ-independent constant, so their gradients coincide and the minimizer is the marginal field, a conditional average of uₜ(x | x₁). Pointwise the two fields differ.

items.prompt: Score-based models are trained on noise-perturbed data at many noise levels rather than on clean data alone. What problem does this solve?
choices: Clean data have no score, because their density is uniform
Scores are poorly estimated in low-density regions where sampling starts
Without noise, score matching needs the data density's normalizing constant
Noise turns the score into a linear function of x that networks fit easily
items.explain: Song and Ermon note that data concentrate near a low-dimensional manifold, where the ambient score is undefined, and that in low-density regions, where Langevin sampling starts, few samples make score estimates inaccurate. Noise fills space with well-estimated scores, and annealing down the noise levels guides samples to the data.

items.prompt: At a lasso solution of ½‖y − Xw‖² + λ‖w‖₁, which condition holds for every feature j with wⱼ = 0?
choices: |xⱼᵀ(y − Xw)| ≤ λ
xⱼᵀ(y − Xw) = 0
|xⱼᵀ(y − Xw)| ≥ λ
|xⱼᵀ y| ≤ λ
items.explain: The subgradient of |wⱼ| at 0 is [−1, 1], so stationarity requires the feature's correlation with the residual to lie in [−λ, λ]. Active features instead satisfy xⱼᵀ(y − Xw) = λ·sign(wⱼ); the last option uses y instead of the residual.

items.prompt: Ridge regression with penalty λ and X having singular values dⱼ. What are its effective degrees of freedom?
choices: Σⱼ λ/(dⱼ² + λ)
The number of columns of X, for every λ
Σⱼ dⱼ²/(dⱼ² + λ)
Σⱼ dⱼ/(dⱼ + λ)
items.explain: Ridge's hat matrix X(XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀ has eigenvalues dⱼ²/(dⱼ² + λ), and degrees of freedom is its trace. It falls from rank(X) (p for full column rank) at λ = 0 toward 0 as λ grows, shrinking weak singular directions most.

items.prompt: PCA is run on raw features measured in very different units (e.g. metres and millimetres). What goes wrong, and what is the usual fix?
choices: Nothing: principal directions are invariant to rescaling any individual feature's units
The covariance matrix becomes non-symmetric; symmetrize it before decomposing
Features with large numeric variance dominate; standardize or use the correlation matrix
Eigenvalues turn negative; take absolute values before ranking components
items.explain: Covariance eigenvectors are not invariant to per-feature scaling, so the feature with the largest numeric variance captures the first component. Standardizing (equivalently, PCA on the correlation matrix) puts features on equal footing.

items.prompt: For the linear map x_{k+1} = Ax, let w be a left eigenvector (wᵀA = λwᵀ) and g(x) = wᵀx. What does the Koopman operator K do to g?
choices: Kg = λ²g
Kg = g/λ
Kg = g for every left eigenvector
Kg = λg
items.explain: Kg(x) = g(Ax) = wᵀAx = λwᵀx = λg(x), so g is a Koopman eigenfunction with eigenvalue λ. For linear systems the Koopman eigenfunctions of linear observables come from the left eigenvectors of A.

items.prompt: A system's largest Lyapunov exponent is 0.5 per unit time. Roughly how long until an initial error of 10⁻⁶ grows to order 1?
choices: About 28 time units
About 2 time units
About 12 time units
About 500,000 time units
items.explain: Errors grow like e^(λt), so t ≈ ln(10⁶)/0.5 ≈ 13.8/0.5 ≈ 28. Predictability horizons grow only logarithmically with measurement precision, so each 10× better initial accuracy buys just ln 10/λ ≈ 4.6 extra time units.

items.prompt: Sutton and Barto call a combination of three ingredients the 'deadly triad', because together they can make value estimates diverge. Which three?
choices: Function approximation, exploration, and discounting
Bootstrapping, on-policy sampling, and a tabular value representation
Off-policy training, Monte Carlo returns, and exploration
Function approximation, bootstrapping, and off-policy training
items.explain: Any two are safe, but with all three, as in Q-learning with linear or neural approximators, semi-gradient TD can diverge (Baird's counterexample). Monte Carlo returns avoid bootstrapping, and tabular methods avoid approximation.
